fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Every Flood Story Is Also a Creation Story", "body": "The premise the hosts build on is that deluge myths and cosmogonies are the same narrative told from opposite ends. Chance Garton leans on George Faber's Origin of Pagan Idolatry, which argues that ancient accounts blend creation and flood so tightly that neither can be told without the other, and reads that through Faber's doctrine of a succession of similar worlds, where each deluge marks the hinge between one age and the next. Garton points to the Greek aeon, translated in scripture as world but meaning age, as the linguistic tell that the Bible is describing cycles rather than a single beginning."}, {"title": "The Two Sources: A Renegade Reverend and a Reluctant Apologist", "body": "The episode runs on two nineteenth century authors. Robert Taylor was a reverend who walked away from the church and turned a scathing wit on scriptural literalism, and his astronomical theological lectures supply the astro theology side. George Faber was a genuine scholar but also a Christian apologist, and Garton notes he conceded that Gentile cosmogonies could not have been borrowed from Moses, that the Egyptian and Hindu systems predate the Israelite exodus, yet still insisted his own tradition stood apart. Garton describes him as ninety nine percent of the way there, with the last piece locked behind belief. Thomas Astle and Edward Lhuyd fill out the reading list."}, {"title": "The Etruscan Thread: Selvans, Salvation, and Baalbek", "body": "Dylan Saccoccio's central argument runs through Italy rather than the Near East. He cites Astle, who held that Saturn, Silenus and Herakles were all names of Noah, and that the Saxons called Hercules Erco. He traces the Latin Silvanus back to the Etruscan Selvans, notes Lhuyd's lexicon glossing the root as salvation and savior, and links Selvans to the caduceus, which he says also appears beside the temple on a Roman coin of Baalbek, the Heliopolis whose inscriptions name a Heliopolitan Jove. On his reading of the abecedaria, Etruscan looks older than Greek, and the Phoenician world's hub sits in Italy."}, {"title": "Reading Myths as Star Maps", "body": "Saccoccio treats the fables as encoded astronomy rather than history. He walks through the Welsh Dylan, son of the wave, born as a lump of flesh and hidden in a chest, which he equates with the ark and with the infant Moses, then ties him to Oannes, the Babylonian fish man whose name he derives toward Johannes and John. Math, whose feet must rest in a virgin's lap when not at war, becomes Virgo opposite Aquarius, and Saint Matthew becomes the royal star Fomalhaut in the southern fish. The sun then passes from man to fish to Aries, the lamb of God."}, {"title": "Plato's Chaos, Seven Sages, and the Divine Right of Kings", "body": "Garton brings in Plato's Timaeus, where the demiurge shapes the cosmos from a pre existing chaos rather than from nothing, and argues that this matches Noah floating the materials of the new world on the deluge before opening the door as the god of gates. He notes Solon among the seven sages, the seven rishis preserved in a boat with Menu in the Ordinances of Menu, the Babylonian Apkallu, and the seven aboard the ark, all pointing at one template. Saccoccio adds the political payoff: the divine right of kings was a chain of custody traced back to Noah as owner of the world."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Every flood story across ancient mythology might be the same story told in different languages. Noah's ark, Kronos, Atlantis, the Hindu deluge, the Babylonian flood. Chance and co-host Dylan Saccoccio walk through the case that they all point to the same archetype and the same hidden meaning.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In this Inner Whirled session: the hidden meaning of Noah's ark, why so many flood heroes share the same traits across unrelated cultures, what Atlantis actually represents in Plato's writing, and the patterns that link the great father figures of world mythology.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Ark, the Egg and the Womb", "body": "Reading from George Faber, Chance lays out why the ark and the egg are interchangeable symbols: the globe pictured as a shell around a great abyss of waters, and the Egyptian fable of Typhon, a personification of the ocean, shutting Osiris in an ark and bursting the mundane egg. The Genesis line that the Lord shut them in becomes the closing of the cosmic egg, and the gods of doors and gates become the opening of the ark. Chance then turns the lens on modern cosmology, calling the Big Bang singularity an egg and modern science a secularized repackaging of the world ages doctrine."}, {"title": "One God Under Many Names", "body": "Chance argues that Bacchus and Noah are one figure: Dionysus reads as God joined to nous, the mind, Bacchus was the first planter of the vine just as Noah taught winemaking, and both were set afloat in an ark. The Orphic hymns call Protogonus twofold and egg born, give Bacchus the same double nature, and make Kronos the power from which the world arose. Augustine's City of God is cited for the claim that the many gods are simply parts of Jove, and Dylan adds the report, via Eusebius citing Porphyry, that the Phoenicians called Kronos Israel, which he reads as the god of time."}, {"title": "The Nile Behind the Flood", "body": "Through Robert Taylor's lectures the hosts trace the deluge to Egypt's yearly inundation. The Nile shows its first rise at the summer solstice, which is why the nativity of John the Baptist sits on the 24th of June; forty days later the flood covers the land, and 150 days counted from that date bring the sun to Aquarius, the just man in whom the world is renewed. The same 150 days falls out of a 360 day year as five winter months of thirty days each. Taylor's verdict, read in full, is that no such person as Noah ever existed and no such deluge ever happened."}, {"title": "Italy as the Land of the Ark", "body": "Dylan works through George Faber's claim that the name Italy comes from Italus, the tauric Noah worshiped alongside the sun, and Chance catches an echo of Ida and the lotus in the name. Faber's list says Italy was first called the land of the Ark and later named from Saturn, whom older scholars equated with Noah. Dylan accepts much of it but reverses the direction: citing Dionysius of Halicarnassus on one people known by two names, he argues the system was carried abroad from Italy rather than into it, and says he has never seen one title Faber claims in any Etruscan inscription he has read."}, {"title": "Oannes and the Head of Wisdom", "body": "Chance reads Oannes, the fish man who rose from the sea to teach the arts of civilization, as Noah spelled backwards. In the Chaldean creation story Belus slays Omorca, the mother of monsters, makes heaven from one half of her and earth from the other, then cuts off his own head so the gods can mix his blood with earth and form mankind, which is why humanity partakes of reason. Chance ties this to the head of John the Baptist, the Templar legends and the oracular head of Mimir, Dylan adds Athena springing from the head of Zeus, and Deucalion becomes the time god."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "Even the modern scientism is just a secularized repackaging of the world ages doctrine.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I haven't had any serious scholars debunk me, and I'm waiting for it.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "All the myths, whether they're about a small destruction or a big destruction, are seeds of, or threads of the same bigger story.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "The sun is the one that measures the time. But life itself is not our creation.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "My experience with people is that the general intention is usually good, even if misguided.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "Does no one find it odd that there is so little authentic Phoenician writing remaining yet such an abundance of Egyptian and Greek writing?", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "How can there be non-existence if there's existence? Seems to me that it's just always been.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I have what I put forward, but I also leave enough wiggle room that I could be entirely wrong and somebody could come forward and show me how I'm wrong.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}]
